## The Project

ExaVerif is an open-core (Apache 2.0) CLI engine for exhaustive verification
of a declared discrete space. A single command consumes a YAML specification
that names fields, their domains, the constraints between them, and an
optional projector. The engine enumerates every point the constraints admit,
classifies it, and reports the result deterministically. The CLI provides
`verify` for classification, `simulate` for a backend recheck, `synth` for
RTL generation and synthesis, and `capabilities` for the layer stack, plus a
`fact decode` utility.

The engine's only knowledge of a target is the spec. A target family enters
through a layout profile, which supplies bit positions when the target packs
its fields into a word, and a backend, which supplies a channel such as
simulation or synthesis. The parser and the classifier are seams as well: a
caller can supply a format or an engine.

RISC-V is one category in that structure: `riscv-r` and `riscv-r4` are
registry entries, and the Spike backend is a simulation backend, both
compiled under the `riscv` feature. The default build includes the target
modules that exist, and `targets` is the aggregate that selects them;
RISC-V is its only member today. The pure generic core is
`--no-default-features`, and `ev capabilities` reports the modules and layers
the binary at hand carries. A spec that names `riscv-r` in the generic core
fails with the rebuild named rather than falling back.

The cores and designs named in this documentation, CVA6 (OpenHW Group), Ibex
(lowRISC), and the Tagma decoder (syntagma), are samples that exercise the
engine. Each is described from that project's own source. The CVA6 encoding
space is re-derived from the hardware decoder mask table at a pinned revision
on every test run. The Ibex mapping is a hand transcription with a pinned
source, and the pin checks the decoder file and the fixture digests, not the
mapping. The Tagma decoder is the sample for the `decompose` projector.

ev emits a structured Fact. Accumulation, supersession, cross-run corpora,
cross-engine comparison, and the design-oracle product belong to the
consumer, ExaSpec. ev's responsibility is the classification itself: complete
over the declared space, reproducible, and correctly addressed.

## The Layer Stack

The engine is organized as layers, each with one responsibility and a
capability seam at its boundary:

| Layer | What it owns | Seam |
|---|---|---|
| Spec space | fields, domains, constraints, projector, optional word layout | `FormatCapable` |
| Layout profile | named bit layouts; `riscv-r`, `riscv-r4`, or a caller's profile | `LayoutRegistry` |
| Classification | the engine that decides each point; structural is the default, naive is the reference | `Classify` |
| Record | `spec_hash`, `point_id`, `id`, `engine`, `claim`, and the verdicts | `Classification` and the Fact envelope |
| Channels | text, JSON, CSV, trace, RTL generation, synthesis, simulation | `ReporterCapable`, `GenerateRtl`, `RunSynthesis`, `RunSimulation` |
| Consumers | accumulation, comparison, supersession, the design oracle | outside ev |

The default build includes the target modules that exist. A target module
adds its layout profile and simulation backend; the generic core
(`--no-default-features`) carries neither, and `ev capabilities` prints the
layer stack for the binary at hand.

A layer can be replaced without changing the ones above or below it. The
classification layer is the most recent seam: `EV_CLASSIFIER=structural` is
the default, `EV_CLASSIFIER=naive` selects the full-expansion reference, and
an imported engine implements the same trait.

## The Spec Space

The unit of verification is the Spec Space, a tripartite model:

- Axes: field domains, each a field with its admissible values.
- Constraints: admissible subspaces over the axes, including oneof, range,
  bitmask, cross, eq, and neq.
- Projector: a mapping from each point of the space to a result value.

The model is itself a complete target specification: axes define the inputs,
constraints define the legal points, and the projector defines the result
mapping. The same YAML compiles to synthesizable SystemVerilog through
`synth`, so exhaustive verification doubles as design generation.

A fourth layer is optional. A word layout maps fields to bit positions when
the target packs them into an instruction, a frame, or a record prefix. The
layout is data: a spec selects a named profile or declares it inline, and a
spec without one has no word. The layout is part of the content address, so
the same fields mapped to different bits are different spaces.

The engine compiles constraints into the enumeration itself. The iterator
visits the valid space directly instead of the full cross product, so a
single spec space verifies in milliseconds, hundreds of times faster than
the standard pipeline. A consumer can run many specs, each an observation
perspective with its own constraint set and projection target; accumulation
and cross-insight belong to that consumer, not to ev.

Identical runs produce identical records, so the classification is
comparable across runs. ev emits the record; a consumer decides how to
accumulate or query it. The structural enumeration is the source of the
speedups measured below, and it is independent of the target: any
deterministic system that maps onto axes, constraints, and a projector
benefits from the same pipeline.

## Why the Gain Is Algorithmic

The speedup is a structural property of the enumeration, not a language
effect. Four points state it, and each has a measurement:

1. Standard `evaluate_all` checks every combination of the full space N. The
   structural classifier visits only the valid space V, with the constraints
   encoded into the iterator.
2. The iterator is index-free. At fixed V, a 100x increase in the raw product
   moves the iterator from 1.64 to 1.93 µs; the cost follows V and the field
   count, not N.
3. `raw_total_combinations` is O(k) and flat in N, because `FieldSpec::len`
   computes a domain's cardinality without materializing it. The measured
   cost is 37 ns across the same 100x range.
4. The structural filter setup is O(sum of domain sizes). It dominates the
   end-to-end time when one field carries a large domain: 3.7 µs to 272 µs as
   that domain grows 100x. The end-to-end pipeline is therefore
   `O(sum domains + V*k)`, not `O(V)` alone.

Both pipelines are Rust in the same release build, measured by the same
harness, so the ratio is the enumeration strategy alone. riscv-dv (UVM and
simulator) and formal tools (SAT and BMC) do not enumerate at all; comparing
against them is comparing different objects. The baseline here is a release
build Rust standard implementation, and the structural gain stands against
that baseline.

Memory is O(V): `evaluate_structural` collects the valid combinations and the
verdicts. The largest committed valid set is 196,608 points. A streaming path
would need a sink-based record API and is deferred until a consumer needs a
valid set that does not fit memory. There is no probabilistic claim: a run
classifies every point of the declared space and nothing else.

## Benchmarks

```{python}
#| label: fig-bench-hero
#| fig-cap: "Verification time: standard evaluate vs structural pipeline. With the structural pipeline integrated into the CLI (issue #42), the CVA6 33M space verifies end-to-end in about 0.2 s; the core pipeline (evaluate_structural) is 36.3 ms, ~360x faster than the naive 13.1 s."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

plt.rcParams.update({"font.family": "sans-serif", "font.size": 9, "figure.dpi": 150})

fixtures = ["Ibex RV32IMCB\n524K raw · 92K valid", "CVA6 XIF full\n33M raw · 196K valid"]
eval_us = [291e3, 13.1e6]    # naive evaluate
struct_us = [9100, 18800]    # structural (count)
cli_us = [16200, 36300]      # evaluate_structural (core)

struct_sp = [e / s for e, s in zip(eval_us, struct_us)]
cli_sp = [e / c for e, c in zip(eval_us, cli_us)]

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.2), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [2, 1]})

x = np.arange(len(fixtures))
w = 0.26
ax1.bar(x - w, eval_us, w, label='evaluate (standard)',
        color='white', edgecolor='#A23B72', linewidth=1.2)
ax1.bar(x, struct_us, w, label='structural (count)',
        color='white', edgecolor='#2E86AB', linewidth=1.2, hatch='///')
ax1.bar(x + w, cli_us, w, label='evaluate_structural (core)',
        color='white', edgecolor='#F18F01', linewidth=1.2, hatch='...')
ax1.set_xticks(x)
ax1.set_xticklabels(fixtures, fontsize=7)
ax1.set_ylabel('Time (µs, log)')
ax1.set_yscale('log')
ax1.legend(fontsize=7, loc='upper left')
ax1.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)
for i in range(len(fixtures)):
    mid = (eval_us[i] * cli_us[i]) ** 0.5
    ax1.annotate(f'{cli_sp[i]:.0f}x', xy=(i + w, mid), fontsize=8, fontweight='bold', ha='center', va='center',
                bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.15', facecolor='white', edgecolor='black', alpha=0.85))
ax1.set_title('Verification Time by Approach', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')

labels = ['Ibex\nstruct', 'Ibex\ncore', 'CVA6\nstruct', 'CVA6\ncore']
all_sp = [struct_sp[0], cli_sp[0], struct_sp[1], cli_sp[1]]
ax2.barh(range(4), all_sp, height=0.5, color='white', edgecolor='black', linewidth=0.8, hatch='///')
ax2.set_yticks(range(4))
ax2.set_yticklabels(labels, fontsize=7)
for i, sp in enumerate(all_sp):
    ax2.text(sp + 15, i, f'{sp:.0f}x', va='center', fontsize=8, fontweight='bold')
ax2.set_xlabel('Speedup vs evaluate')
ax2.set_title('Speedup', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
ax2.set_xlim(0, max(all_sp) * 1.15)
ax2.tick_params(labelsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Scaling: O(N) vs O(V)

```{python}
#| label: fig-scaling-main
#| fig-cap: "Scaling across fixtures: evaluate runs in O(N), the structural iterator visits O(V). The gap widens as valid density drops; CVA6 full (0.6% density) shows ~700x."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

plt.rcParams.update({"font.family": "sans-serif", "font.size": 9, "figure.dpi": 150})

raw_sizes = [27, 32768, 524288, 33554432]
valid_sizes = [27, 20480, 92160, 196608]
eval_times_us = [4.87, 5990, 291000, 13.1e6]
struct_times_us = [2.86, 3020, 9100, 18800]
labels = ['Small\n27', 'Medium\n32K', 'Ibex\n524K', 'CVA6\n33M']

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.plot(raw_sizes, eval_times_us, 'o-', color='#A23B72', linewidth=1.5,
        markerfacecolor='white', markeredgecolor='#A23B72', markersize=6, label='evaluate (standard) O(N)')
ax.plot(valid_sizes, struct_times_us, 's-', color='#2E86AB', linewidth=1.5,
        markerfacecolor='white', markeredgecolor='#2E86AB', markersize=6, label='structural classifier O(V)')
for (rx, ty), (vx, sy), lab in zip(zip(raw_sizes, eval_times_us), zip(valid_sizes, struct_times_us), labels):
    sp = ty / sy
    ax.annotate(f'{sp:.0f}x', xy=(rx, ty), fontsize=7, fontweight='bold',
                xytext=(rx * 2.0, ty * 0.5),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='gray', linewidth=0.5))
ax.set_xscale('log')
ax.set_yscale('log')
ax.set_xlabel('Combinations (log scale)')
ax.set_ylabel('Time (µs, log scale)')
ax.set_title('Scaling: O(N) vs O(V)', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Speedup follows approximately `k / D` (D = valid density): sparse spaces gain
the most (CVA6 full 0.6% density, ~700x; Ibex 17.6%, 32x; dense spaces 1-2x).

## Fixture Speedups

| Fixture | Raw | Valid | evaluate | structural | Speedup |
|---------|----:|------:|---------:|-----------:|--------:|
| Small | 27 | 27 | 4.87 µs | 2.86 µs | 1.7x |
| Medium | 32,768 | 20,480 | 5.99 ms | 3.02 ms | 2.0x |
| Tagma | 65,536 | 11,172 | 9.74 ms | 5.94 ms | N/A (reference) |
| Ibex R-type | 524,288 | 92,160 | 291 ms | 9.10 ms | 32x |
| CVA6 R4 | 16,384 | 2,560 | 3.14 ms | 250 µs | 13x |
| CVA6 full | 33,554,432 | 196,608 | 13.1 s | 18.8 ms | ~700x |
| CVA6 full (evaluate_structural) | 33,554,432 | 196,608 | 13.1 s | 36.3 ms | 361x |

The two synthetic scaling axes in `benches/bench.rs` isolate the property.
At fixed V, the iterator stays flat as the raw space grows; the filter setup
grows with the domain size. At fixed V with a growing field count k, the
end-to-end cost is linear in k: 0.97, 1.91, 3.69, and 8.15 µs for 4, 8, 16,
and 32 fields. `cargo bench -- scaling` reproduces both.

## Status

The engine is the default path. `ev verify` runs the structural classifier;
the naive pipeline is selectable with `EV_CLASSIFIER=naive` and is the
reference the tests compare against. Every record names its engine and claim
class, and every point carries a coordinate identity that excludes the
verdict.

The RISC-V samples are two reports:

- CVA6 CV-X-IF (OpenHW): the 33.5M space derives from the hardware decoder
  mask table at a pinned revision and is re-derived by a gate. Report:
  [CVA6 CV-X-IF Report](/projects/ev/cva6.html).
- Ibex RV32IMCB (lowRISC): the 524,288-point space is a hand transcription
  from `ibex_decoder.sv` at a pinned revision; the pin checks the decoder and
  the fixture digests, not the mapping. Report:
  [Ibex RV32IMCB Report](/projects/ev/ibex.html).

### Limits

- Exhaustive coverage grows exponentially with the number of fields and their
  domains. The speedup depends on valid-space density, not raw size.
- The structural filter setup is O(sum of domain sizes). A single very large
  domain costs its size even though the valid set is small.
- Memory is O(V). A valid set that does not fit memory needs a streaming path,
  which is not implemented.
- Compile-time configuration spaces are out of scope. A configuration selects
  which instructions exist; a spec models one configuration and states the
  parameter binding it assumes.
- The Ibex mapping is a transcription, not a derived artifact. A consumer that
  needs a mechanically derived Ibex mapping must derive it outside ev.
- Counts are field-value combinations and equal distinct instruction words
  where no enable_mask collapses them.
